title: There are five people in my family
title_target: ကျွန်မ မိသားစု ငါးယောက် ရှိပါတယ် — cha.ma. mee.tha:-soo. nga:-yowk shee.-ba-dè
goal: Name family members and say how many there are — and meet two surprises at once: one verb that means both "there is" and "have", and words for younger siblings that change with the speaker's gender.
bekal: name the members of your immediate family
use ရှိတယ် for "there is" and "have"
count people with the classifier ယောက်
choose ညီ, မောင်, ညီမ, or နှမ correctly
ask how many with ဘယ်နှစ်ယောက်လဲ

dialogs.title: စကားပြော — Looking at family photos
dialogs.intro: Mya Mya shows Ani her family photo album. Notice two things: the word ရှိတယ် is used for both "there is" and "have", and Ani and Mya Mya use different words for "younger sister" — not because the sisters are different, but because the speakers are.

grammars.title: ⚠️ ရှိတယ် — one word for "there is" and "have"
body: Burmese has no special verb for "have". It uses ရှိတယ် (*shee.-dè*), which literally means "exist, there is". Ownership is expressed by naming the owner first, plus the marker မှာ ("at").

head: Burmese
Say it
Literal translation
Actual meaning
rows: ပိုက်ဆံ ရှိတယ်
ကျွန်မမှာ ပိုက်ဆံ ရှိတယ်
အိမ်မှာ ရေ ရှိတယ်
ပိုက်ဆံ မရှိဘူး

after: ⚠️ Age uses ရှိတယ် too, not "be": အသက် ၁၆ နှစ် ရှိပါတယ် — literally "age sixteen years exists". Translating "I am sixteen" word for word from English produces a sentence nobody in Myanmar would ever say.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Younger siblings follow the SPEAKER'S gender, not the sibling's
body: Just like ကျွန်တော်/ကျွန်မ in unit 1, the words for brothers and sisters depend on **who is speaking**. This trips up almost every beginner, because in English a sister is a sister no matter who's talking.

head: The person meant
If the speaker is a man
If the speaker is a woman

after: Notice the pattern: **older siblings are the same for everyone; younger ones differ.** So you only need to learn the four words in the third and fourth rows.

The easiest way to remember: women use မောင် and နှမ — two words you'll also meet as parts of people's names. Men use ညီ and ညီမ, and ညီမ means "younger sister" because the ending မ marks a woman, just as in ဆရာမ.

grammars.title: Counting people: ယောက် and ဦး
body: Counting in Burmese uses a fixed order: **noun — number — classifier**, a bit like English "three head of cattle". For people, the classifier is ယောက်; for respected people, ဦး.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: လူ တစ်ယောက်
လူ နှစ်ယောက်
ဆရာ နှစ်ဦး
ဘယ်နှစ်ယောက်လဲ

after: ⚠️ တစ် (one) and နှစ် (two) **change form** before a classifier: တစ်ယောက် is read *ta.yowk*, not *tik-yowk*, and နှစ်ယောက် is read *hna.yowk*, not *hnik-yowk*. This happens with every classifier, so learn it once here and it holds forever.

grammars.title: ဆိုတော့ and လို့ — linking reasons and names
body: Two small words from the dialogue that will keep coming back. Both go **after** the part they refer to.

head: Word

Example
rows: မိန်းကလေး ဆိုတော့ — since (she's) a girl
နှမလို့ ခေါ်တယ် — is called နှမ
ဘာဖြစ်လို့လဲ

after: ပေါ့ (*paw.*) at the end of the dialogue's last line is a little word meaning "I suppose, right?". It softens a conclusion so it doesn't sound like a lecture — very common, and it instantly makes your Burmese sound natural.

blocks.text: In Myanmar, older people are almost never called by their name alone. Family terms are used with anyone — market sellers, taxi drivers, neighbors — much as some English speakers say "auntie" or "uncle" to family friends, only far more widely.

head: Burmese
Say it
English
rows: ခင်ပွန်း · ဇနီး
title for a man · woman of similar age

blocks.title: How to address people you've just met
items: **Same age or a little younger:** ကို (*koh*) before a man's name, မ (*ma.*) before a woman's name. Ko Zaw and Ma Mya in this book follow this pattern.
**Clearly older:** ဦး (*oo:*) for men, ဒေါ် (*dò*) for women. The department head in unit 3's dialogue is addressed as ဒေါ်ခင်.
**Strangers in the street:** ဦးလေး (uncle) and အဒေါ် (aunt) are always safe and always warmly received. ⚠️ Calling a clearly older person by their bare name sounds rude, even from a foreigner.
